title: Sisera's mother at the window (Judges 5:28–30)
hookLine: the song pauses on the enemy's mother, waiting; later tradition hears her cries in the shofar's notes

lines: WHY IS HIS CHARIOT SO LONG IN COMING?
cards: Through a lattice, a woman watches an empty road. The song of victory has been loud: the stars fighting from their courses, the river sweeping the enemy away, Jael blessed in her tent.
Then, near the very end, it goes quiet and moves somewhere unexpected. Not to Israel's camp. To the enemy's house.
"The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?"

teach.b: You know something she doesn't. Her son is already dead, in a stranger's tent. She's still at the window.
Her wisest ladies try to comfort her, and she answers herself with the same words: they must be dividing the spoil. A girl or two for every man.
Dyed cloth for Sisera, embroidered on both sides, for the necks of the victors. The song doesn't make her innocent.

Her comfort is plunder, and captive women from someone else's town, exactly the kind of victory her son had been winning over Israel. And still the song stays with her: the window, the lattice, the questions, the waiting.
Then it ends with a line of its own: "So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD."
The song holds both at once: a victory it celebrates, and a mother it can't stop looking at. Jewish tradition kept looking too. Remember teruah, the great shout at Jericho?
It's also a shofar call. When the Talmud asks what the teruah of Rosh Hashanah should sound like, it reaches for this verse. The word for her crying, vateyabev, is the clue.
The rabbis ask whether her cry was a groan or a sob, and the shofar sounds both. Later tradition hears her cries in the shofar's notes.
On the day of judgment, in the middle of the new year's prayers, the sound that wakes the congregation carries the cry of the enemy's mother.
Nobody has to excuse what her son did to remember that she waited at a window for someone who wasn't coming home.

how: Jews read Sisera's mother in the Song of Deborah, and the Talmud's discussion of the shofar's teruah sound in tractate Rosh Hashanah draws on the verse about her crying, a link remembered when the shofar is blown on Rosh Hashanah.

o: and she wailed: the cry of Sisera's mother
and she waited: Jael at her tent door
and she sang: Deborah's song of victory

games.q: the other mother waits — tap the pairs.
p: the spoil she imagined for Sisera
the shofar sound linked to her cry

s: the Song of Deborah never mentions the enemy's family
near its end it stops at Sisera's mother, waiting at the window.
Sisera's mother comforts herself with thoughts of spoil
they must be dividing the prey: girls for the men, dyed cloth for Sisera.
the Talmud links the shofar's sound to her cry
asking what the teruah should sound like, it points to this verse: she wailed.

games.q: you're writing the victory song. Sisera is dead, the war is won. how do you end it?
o: with the people dancing in the streets.
at the enemy's house, where his mother waits.
with a list of the fallen.
games.why: the song goes to Sisera's mother at the window, asking why his chariot is so late, and only then ends its praise.

practice: Bring to mind someone on the other side of something: an argument you won, a rivalry, a team that lost, a group your people disagree with, a neighbor you're at odds with.
You don't have to change your mind about anything; just find the person at their window, and ask who is waiting for them and what they might be afraid of tonight.
Let the picture stay a moment, without excusing anything, and without looking away.

wordCard.voice: vateyabev. The cry of Sisera's mother at the window, waiting for a chariot that won't come, which tradition hears in the shofar. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and she wailed, said of Sisera's mother in Judges 5:28; the Talmud uses it to describe the shofar's teruah.

carryVoice: Your line: the other mother waits. The song holds both, the victory and the grief. See you tomorrow.
